title: Cost of waiting 5 years to start your Roth
audience: Young adults putting off retirement savings because "they have time"
thesis: Starting your Roth at 25 vs 30 isn't 5 years of catch-up — it's 5 years of compounding you'll never recover.

concepts.label: The compounding gap
concepts.body: Starting at 25 instead of 30, contributing $7,500 a year at a 7% real return, ages into a $1.6 million difference by age 65. The early starter puts in $187,500 over 40 years; the late starter puts in $262,500 over 35 years — and yet the early starter ends up with more.
concepts.source: Future-value of an annuity, FV = PMT × [((1 + r)^n - 1) / r] with r=0.07

concepts.label: The five lost years
concepts.body: The five years you wait are not just five years of contributions you missed. They're five years of compounding on those contributions that you will never get back — and the missing earnings compound too.
concepts.source: Compounding window math; first-five-years acceleration effect

concepts.label: The 'catch-up' myth
concepts.body: Doubling contributions later doesn't catch you up. To match a 25-year-old's Roth by 65, a 30-year-old has to contribute roughly 25% more per year, every year, for the rest of their working life.
concepts.source: Back-solving FV annuity equation for required PMT

sources: Future-value of an annuity formula (standard finance textbook)
